rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succeeding passage warns the Quraysh through accounts of the humiliating punishments inflicted on earlier peoples who rejected their messengers.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, in order to warn the Quraysh the details of the humiliating punishment meted out to some previous nations which rejected their respective messenger are presented.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 37 returns to the creation arguments in 41:9–12; intervening warnings, reminders, and assurances leave the discourse coherent.
rows.anchor: In verses 9 to 12 of this sūr ah arguments are drawn from the creation of the heavens and the earth on the doctrines of monotheism and the Hereafter.

words: وَمِنْ ءَايَٰتِهِ ٱلَّيْلُ وَٱلنَّهَارُ وَٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night, day, sun, and moon are signs of their Creator; their cycles, rising, and setting show they are subordinate, not gods or partners.
rows.anchor: Their alternation and rising and setting bear witness to their subservience. From their very existence, they bear evidence that they are neither God nor His partners in any way

words: وَمِنْ ءَايَٰتِهِ ٱلَّيْلُ وَٱلنَّهَارُ وَٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fitted these celestial bodies into the universe's machinery to perform their assigned service at His command.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has fitted them as spare-parts in the machinery of this universe, and at His bidding are

words: وَمِنْ ءَايَٰتِهِ ٱلَّيْلُ وَٱلنَّهَارُ وَٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They carry out their assigned service; they are signs of God's power, wisdom, mercy, and providence, and only a few among many such signs.
rows.anchor: discharging the service assigned to them. After this testimony of theirs, it is mere foolishness and ignorance to regard them God or His partners.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worshipping these created signs belittles both God and the worshippers; only their Creator is worthy of worship and made them serve humanity.
rows.anchor: those who worship them not only belittle God but also their own selves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prostration here stands for worship because it is worship's most prominent outward manifestation.
rows.anchor: The word prostration here connotes worship because it is the most prominent manifestation of worship.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition singles out sun and moon worship because idolatrous peoples have worshipped them in every age.
rows.anchor: It is specially stressed that people should not worship the sun and the moon because idolatrous nations have worshipped them in every age.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “created them” refers to all the objects just mentioned.
rows.anchor: refers to all the objects mentioned earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pure worship of God requires prostrating to no one besides Him; prostration is worship's greatest manifestation and belongs to God alone.
rows.anchor: one can only fulfil the right of purely worshipping God if none except Him is prostrated to.

rows.speaker: idolaters of Arabia
rows.claim: They worshipped other beings believing them to be means of gaining God's favour, and viewed that worship as equivalent to worshipping God.
rows.anchor: the idolaters of Arabia worshipped other things besides God, it was because they thought that these things are a means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording refutes that rationale: worship belongs to God alone, with no one sharing its distinctive acts.
rows.anchor: These words refute this claim: God should be worshipped alone such that no one should even share the specific signs of this worship with anyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If arrogance makes the people ignore the Prophet and claim deafness to his message, he should leave them to themselves.
rows.anchor: if because of arrogance they are not paying heed to him and haughtily remark that their ears are deaf to what he is saying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their refusal to worship does not affect God; He has no concern for them, and the Prophet should likewise show no concern.
rows.anchor: God has not the slightest concern for them; the Prophet (sws) too should show no concern for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels in God's presence praise Him night and day and never tire.
rows.anchor: The angels that are found in His presence are busy extolling Him day and night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those near your Lord” means the angels collectively, not merely angels who remain constantly in God's presence, since the described quality belongs to all angels.
rows.anchor: connote the angels in their collective capacity; they do not refer to the ones who always remain in the presence of the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' nearness to God is expressed in relation to human beings and jinn.
rows.anchor: are meant to express the nearness the angels have with God with regard to man and jinn.

none: bare heading and copyright apparatus only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh's arrogance stems from denying the afterlife, so warnings of it seem like jest to them.
rows.anchor: the real reason behind the arrogance and haughtiness of the Quraysh is alluded to: they do not believe in any concept of afterlife.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage presents intellectual and historical evidence for reward and punishment, then depicts the fates of believers and disbelievers; God treats them differently with complete justice.
rows.anchor: logical as well as historical arguments in favour of reward and punishment are briefly referred to. It is mentioned in detail that God will not deal equally between those who spent their lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section presents the Qur'an's clear Arabic revelation as a favor to Quraysh, echoing the sūrah's opening praise and affirming that it fully conveys the truth.
rows.anchor: the sūrah began with a note on the exaltedness of the Qur’ ān and it ends on the same note. In it, the Quraysh are warned that the Almighty has equipped the Qur’ ān with all essential requisites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecting this favor brings the fate of those who rejected God's messengers; if they choose to await punishment, the Prophet is told to await their evil day too.
rows.anchor: if instead of benefiting from this favour, these people want to wait for the punishment, then he too should wait for the advent of this evil day for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context selects the favorable sense of the term under discussion, as in 8:17 where it is paired with “goodly.”
rows.anchor: Contextual indications show that in this verse this word is used in the first of these meanings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term refers to favors granted to the Israelites during the desert crossing and life there, the conquest of Palestine, and later periods; their details occur in Sūrah al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: The reference is to the favours which the Almighty granted them in a variety of ways while they were crossing the desert

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming section identifies disbelief in life after death as the cause of Quraysh rebellion and heedlessness of the future.
rows.anchor: the real reason for the rebelliousness of the Quraysh is highlighted: they do not imagine that there is life after this worldly existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section first offers intellectual and natural arguments for reward and punishment, then describes the fate of believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: first the intellectual and natural arguments which substantiate the law of reward and punishment are cited. After this, the fate of both the believers and the disbelievers is depicted.

rows.speaker: these people
rows.claim: They insist the warning of Judgment is a bluff: death happens only once in this world, with no subsequent life or death.
rows.anchor: these people very emphatically claim that the threat of the Day of judgement is mere bluff. Death is only faced once – and that is in this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To support their denial, they demand that believers bring a forefather back to life, saying they would then accept the afterlife.
rows.anchor: they would demand of the believers to bring back any of their forefathers to life if they were truthful in saying that there is life after death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an calls this their sole argument and leaves it unanswered because its nonsensical absurdity needs no refutation.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has regarded this to be their only argument, and after referring to it has just ignored it and not even refuted it.
